theme: A. Theory: how a fuel price becomes a consumer price
method: Leontief input-output price model
findings: The price of each good covers the cost of its inputs plus value added, so a rise in the price of one input (such as fuel) raises every price in proportion to the input's direct and indirect cost share.

theme: A. Theory: how a fuel price becomes a consumer price
method: Non-parametric regression of net benefit ratios (budget-share approach to welfare effects of price changes)
findings: The first-order welfare effect of a price change equals the household's net budget share times the price change; higher rice prices help net-selling farm households and hurt net buyers, so the effect depends on what each household buys and sells.

theme: A. Theory: how a fuel price becomes a consumer price
sample: Review; mainly United States since the 1970s
method: Survey of theory and evidence
findings: Energy price shocks affect consumers directly, through energy purchases, and indirectly, through costs and spending; their effects on inflation and output depend on whether they come from supply or demand, and have waned since the 1980s.

theme: A. Theory: how a fuel price becomes a consumer price
sample: United States and other industrial economies, 1970s-2000s
method: Structural VARs and a new-Keynesian model
findings: Oil shocks had much smaller effects on inflation and output in the 2000s than in the 1970s: second-round wage effects were weaker, monetary policy more credible and the oil share of production smaller.

theme: A. Theory: how a fuel price becomes a consumer price
sample: Global crude oil market; United States, 1973-2007
method: Structural VAR separating oil supply, aggregate demand and oil-specific demand shocks
findings: Not all oil price shocks are alike: supply, global-demand and oil-specific demand shocks have different effects on prices and activity, which explains why simple regressions on oil prices are unstable.

theme: A. Theory: how a fuel price becomes a consumer price
method: Bayesian structural VAR with uncertain identifying assumptions
findings: Oil supply disruptions explain more of historical oil price movements than earlier estimates; supply shocks reduce world activity after a lag, demand shocks do not.

theme: A. Theory: how a fuel price becomes a consumer price
sample: Oil market and United States economy, 1970s-2010s
method: High-frequency identification from OPEC announcements; VARs and local projections
findings: Negative oil supply news raises oil prices immediately and lowers output; prices and inflation expectations rise, showing a strong expectations channel.

theme: B. Evidence on pass-through to inflation
method: Local projections on a new global retail fuel price database
findings: A one-cent rise in crude oil per litre raises retail gasoline prices by about 1.2 cents at peak, after about six months; pass-through varies by region and is larger for increases than decreases.

theme: B. Evidence on pass-through to inflation
method: Panel data analysis of the pass-through of international to domestic fuel prices
findings: Pass-through is higher when world price changes are moderate and less volatile and when pricing rules are flexible; depreciation and cheaper fuel in neighbouring countries reduce it.

theme: B. Evidence on pass-through to inflation
method: Local projections, panel
findings: A 10% rise in global oil prices raises domestic inflation by about 0.4 pp on impact, fading within two years; the effect is asymmetric and has declined over time, largely because of better monetary policy.

theme: B. Evidence on pass-through to inflation
sample: 31 advanced and 61 emerging and developing economies
method: Panel and country regressions of inflation on commodity price shocks
findings: Fuel price shocks have larger and more persistent effects in oil-intensive economies and where inflation was already high.

theme: B. Evidence on pass-through to inflation
sample: 122 countries, monthly, 2000-2019 (incl. the Philippines in the developing group)
method: Local projections with Teulings-Zubanov correction; quintile CPIs rebuilt from survey weights
findings: Retail fuel prices pass through to inflation (peak about 0.04 pp per 1% in advanced and 0.02 pp in developing economies); crude prices understate it; the effect on the richest-to-poorest quintile CPI ratio is progressive.

theme: B. Evidence on pass-through to inflation
sample: Nine developing Asian economies, 2007-2008 price spike
method: Empirical pass-through analysis of global food and oil prices to consumer prices
findings: The pass-through of global food and oil prices to consumer prices was limited; subsidies and price controls reduced or delayed it.

theme: B. Evidence on pass-through to inflation
method: Local projections of inflation on oil, food and rice price shocks
findings: Global oil and food shocks have significant and persistent effects on Philippine inflation; second-round effects of oil are as large as its direct effects; core inflation responds asymmetrically to oil shocks.

theme: B. Evidence on pass-through to inflation
sample: Philippine provinces, monthly, 1996-2024 (with Indonesia, Thailand, India)
method: Quantile regression
findings: Energy and rice prices raise inflation more when inflation is high; inflation targeting and rice tariffication weakened the rice effect, especially in high-poverty and rice-deficit areas.

theme: C. Who bears fuel price changes
sample: Review of country studies, developing countries
method: Survey of incidence studies (direct and indirect effects)
findings: A fuel price increase lowers real incomes by a similar percentage across income groups, more than half of it through indirect effects; in absolute terms the richest fifth receives about six times more subsidy than the poorest.

theme: C. Who bears fuel price changes
method: Survey of incidence studies
findings: Newer studies confirm that higher-income households capture most of the benefits of fuel subsidies, which worsens inequality.

theme: C. Who bears fuel price changes
method: Computable general equilibrium model
findings: Removing fuel import subsidies raises GDP but can lower household incomes, especially of the poor; transfers to poor households can offset the losses.

theme: C. Who bears fuel price changes
method: Incidence analysis with concentration curves
findings: Petrol subsidies flow mainly to richer households and kerosene subsidies are more evenly shared; overall the top fifth receives about twice the benefit of the bottom fifth.

theme: C. Who bears fuel price changes
method: Input-output incidence analysis of carbon pricing
findings: Carbon pricing is on average progressive in countries with incomes below about USD 15,000 per person, because energy budget shares rise and then fall with income.

theme: C. Who bears fuel price changes
method: Household-level analysis of the effects of rice and fuel price increases
findings: The impact of higher rice and fuel prices differs by sector of employment, urbanity, income group and location; there are gainers as well as losers, and better targeting of mitigation programmes is needed.

theme: C. Who bears fuel price changes
method: Household panel analysis of programme participation
findings: The Raskin rice subsidy reaches the poor more than the non-poor, but take-up is regressive within the poor: the poorest households buy less subsidised rice.

theme: D. Do the poor face different inflation?
method: Polling data and pooled cross-country regressions
findings: The poor are more likely than the rich to name inflation as a top concern; high inflation lowers the income share of the bottom quintile and the real minimum wage and raises poverty.

theme: D. Do the poor face different inflation?
method: Household-specific price indices from expenditure data
findings: Inflation differs substantially across households; the cost of living of poor households is the most sensitive to fluctuations in gasoline prices.

theme: D. Do the poor face different inflation?
method: Household-level price indices
findings: Household inflation rates are very dispersed, mostly because households pay different prices for the same kinds of goods; lower-income households face higher inflation.

theme: D. Do the poor face different inflation?
method: Survey
findings: Inflation rates decline with household income in the United States; measuring this needs granular prices, because aggregation hides differences in what each group buys within categories.

theme: D. Do the poor face different inflation?
sample: Philippines, 2006-2008; household survey and provincial prices
method: Non-parametric welfare analysis of food price changes
findings: Food price increases raised poverty, and the poorest households were hit hard whether or not they farmed.

theme: E. Rice, food prices and policy in Asia
method: Policy analysis of food price stabilisation
findings: Stabilising rice prices supports growth and food security; a rice price spike caused by an import ban pushed about 4 million Indonesians into poverty.

theme: E. Rice, food prices and policy in Asia
sample: Philippines; global rice model and FIES
method: Simulation of rice tariffication on prices and household welfare
findings: Rice tariffication lowered consumer and producer rice prices; most households, and the poorest quintiles and regions most, gained, while net-selling rice farmers lost.

theme: E. Rice, food prices and policy in Asia
method: Market review and microsimulation
findings: Rice tariffication lowered palay and retail rice prices; the lower palay price raises poverty only slightly, and targeted transfers to affected farmers can offset it.
